title: Reading lessons, Hi Lama, and help from Manny Klein and Dave Klein
summary: A teacher wanted to hear him play rather than teach reading, so Edison learned from studio colleagues, and Dave Klein kept him working.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Oh, yes, yes, yes. So I went to -- a trumpet player, I was asking, who can I go to around here to give me some lessons to improve my reading, you know. And I just wanted to learn how to sit down like the rest of the guys and come right in, pull my horn out, tune up and look over and play it.
Well, they sent me to a guy named Hi Lama.
How do you spell that? H-y?

Yeah, L-e- -- I forget how to spell his last name. But he was a good teacher here at the time. And he was recommended to me by the studio musicians. So I went in his studio and he said, 'Okay,' you know, just like a doctor's examining you, he said, 'Play.' So I started playing and playing and he asked me what I wanted to do. I told him.
So he -- I played and played. I played for about 45 minutes. And I said, 'Well, what do you think?' He said, 'well,

if I could play like that, I wouldn't want to learn how to read." You know. I can understand the way you're thinking but can't you understand the way I'm thinking? "I want to improve myself in this music business where I won't have to depend if I can -- naturally, I can play jazz, that comes natural to me. But you have to be taught the other phase of the business if you want to be successful out here in the studios."

So that was the end of that session with him because he wanted to hear me play, see. And I wanted to learn what he had to offer me, you know. But I just kept asking and asking and asking around, how do you play this. And those guys were absolutely fantastic to me, to give me their knowledge.
So it came more, then, from the guys in the band?

In the band, yes. And Manny had a brother at the time, Dave Klein, who was a contractor here in Los Angeles. And he was an ex-trumpet player. And he just used to keep me working all the time. And I became one of his favorite trumpet players, you know.
Well, you fell on your feet very nicely.
